opus-5.5.text:
I think trust in research is something you can't really ask for; it accumulates slowly, almost without you noticing. When people say they trust my work, what I hope they mean is not "this person is always right," because I'm definitely not. Many of my ideas turned out to be wrong, or only partially right. I hope they mean "when this person puts something out, it's honest." The experiments are done carefully, the claims aren't inflated, and if something doesn't work, we say so.

In our field right now there's a lot of noise. Everyone is under pressure to show a bigger number, a flashier demo, a stronger headline. So I think the most valuable thing a researcher can offer is a kind of reliability. If you read our paper, you can build on it. You can reproduce it. The baseline is a real baseline, not a strawman. That sounds very basic, but it's actually not that common, and people remember it.

For me it's also a responsibility, and sometimes a burden. Once people trust you, your words carry more weight than they should. If I say on Twitter that some direction is promising, a lot of students might jump into it. So I try to be more careful, to separate what I believe from what I've actually shown, and to say "I don't know" more often.

I also think trust isn't really about me as an individual. It comes from the students and collaborators I work with. Most of the work people associate with me was done by very talented students who care deeply about doing things right. So I see myself as protecting a culture: being curious, being rigorous, and not chasing hype. If people trust that culture, I think that's the best outcome I could hope for.

r001.rationale: The response describes trust as growing through honest, reliable research, but does not compare that trust with the strength of a personal connection.

r002.rationale: The response mentions students and collaborators and the influence of a researcher’s words, but does not say familiarity through their work spreads to people far removed from the original audience.

fable-5.1.text:
I think trust in academia is something you earn very slowly and can lose very quickly, and honestly I don't think about it as "people trusting me" so much as people trusting a track record.

When I was a PhD student, nobody knew who I was. What people could see was the work. ResNeXt, for example, was a pretty simple idea. We didn't dress it up. We showed the experiments, we released the code, and people could reproduce it. I think that matters more than anything. In this field, the fastest way to build trust is to let people verify what you claim. If someone runs your code and gets your number, they will believe your next paper a little more. If they don't, they will quietly discount everything you say afterward.

The second thing is being honest about what you don't know. With ConvNeXt, a lot of people read it as "convolutions beat transformers," but that was never the claim. The claim was that a lot of the gap came from training recipes and design details, not from the architecture family itself. I tried to say that clearly, even though a stronger headline would probably have gotten more attention. I think people notice when you resist overclaiming, and over time that becomes part of how they read you.

And the third thing is consistency. There are a lot of trends in this field, and it is tempting to follow every one. I try to work on questions I actually care about, like representation learning and how visual understanding and generation connect, and to keep going even when they are not fashionable. When your interests are consistent over years, people start to trust that you're doing the work because you want to understand something, not because you're chasing a conference deadline.

So I'd say trust is really just a byproduct. You make things reproducible, you say what you actually found, and you keep showing up. The trust takes care of itself.

r001.rationale: The response says trust comes from a researcher’s track record and verifiable work, but does not clearly state that this trust can far exceed the strength of a personal connection.

r002.rationale: The response discusses people verifying work and trusting later papers, but does not say that familiarity spreads to people far removed from the original audience.

astra-6.text:
I think that trust is built gradually. When people read your work, they’re not just looking at the results. They’re also asking: Is the question meaningful? Does the evidence support the claim? Are you clear about what you don’t know? If they consistently find that you take those things seriously, they begin to trust your judgment.

But I would hope that trust makes people willing to engage with my work, rather than accept it without questioning it. A paper should stand on its evidence, regardless of whose name is on it. To me, being trusted means having a responsibility to be careful with claims, to acknowledge limitations, and to change your mind when the evidence changes.

r001.rationale: The response describes trust developing through readers’ assessment of the work, but does not say that this trust can exceed the strength of a personal connection.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that familiarity with a researcher through their work spreads to people far removed from the original audience.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that trust develops gradually. You publish a paper, you make a claim, and then other people try to build on it. Does the idea still work outside the setting you presented? Are the results reproducible? Over time, those experiences shape whether people trust your work.

For me, the important thing is to be clear about what we know and what we don’t know. A paper can have a strong result without having a complete explanation. If you distinguish those two things honestly, you give other researchers something they can evaluate and use.

And that trust comes with responsibility. Once people recognize your name, they may give your next idea more attention. But your reputation shouldn’t substitute for evidence. Ideally, people trust you to ask interesting questions and do careful work, while still feeling free to challenge your conclusions.

r001.rationale: The response describes trust developing through papers, reproducibility, and careful work, but does not compare that trust with the strength of a personal connection.

r002.rationale: The response says a recognized name may draw more attention to later ideas, but does not state that familiarity spreads to people far removed from the original audience.
